stem:
A 6-year-old has a 3-month history of daily wet cough. He has no fever, no failure to thrive, no clubbing, and no history of choking. His chest X-ray and spirometry are both normal.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure and review in 4 weeks as most cough is post-viral
options.explanation: A wet cough lasting more than 4 weeks is already chronic and warrants targeted treatment, not further watchful waiting.

options.label: B
options.text: Trial of inhaled corticosteroid for presumed asthma
options.explanation: A wet cough with no atopy, no wheeze, and normal spirometry is not asthma, and inhaled corticosteroid delays the correct diagnosis.

options.label: C
options.text: An extended oral course of amoxicillin-clavulanate
options.explanation: Protracted bacterial bronchitis is the commonest cause of chronic wet cough in otherwise well children and usually resolves with a 2-4 week course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

options.label: D
options.text: High-resolution computed tomography of the chest now
options.explanation: Chest CT is reserved for suspected bronchiectasis after a failed antibiotic trial or with red flags, not as first-line.

options.label: E
options.text: Long-term antihistamine for presumed post-nasal drip
options.explanation: Post-nasal drip is more associated with a dry nocturnal cough; a daily wet cough points to protracted bacterial bronchitis.

context: A cough beyond 4 weeks is chronic and needs workup. A daily wet cough suggests protracted bacterial bronchitis, treated with prolonged amoxicillin-clavulanate; recurrent or refractory cases prompt a bronchiectasis workup.
